title: Ten Years of the Revenue of the Ancient Colonists: What the Ordonnance Said and What the Ceremony Left Out
participants: M. Guyot, President of the Haitian Senate
Caisse générale des Dépôts et des Consignations
Former colonists of Saint-Domingue claiming indemnity

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim is the whole instrument and it is Article 2: "The present inhabitants of the French part of St. Domingo shall pay into the Caisse [générale des Dépôts et] des Consignations of France, in five equal instalments, from year to year, the first of which will become due on the 31st of December, 1825, the sum of 150,000,000 of francs, destined to indemnify the ancient colonists who shall claim an indemnity." Thirty millions of dollars at the day's rate, a fifth of it due within eight months of the ordonnance being signed — and, as an American paper reported, "not the maximum demanded by France at the commencement of the negotiation ... f[if]ty millions were asked".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise is in Article 1, and it is a tariff rather than a tribute: the ports are "open to the commerce of all nations" with duties "equal and uniform for all flags except for the French flag, in favor of which these duties shall be reduced one half." The customs regime of a newly independent state was written into the act recognising it, permanently advantaging the former metropole. The following year's Convention narrowed and specified that advantage further, limiting it to "French manufactures and produce, the property of Frenchmen, imp[ort]ed in French bottoms direct from France".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is the order of the three articles, and it survives in the text. Article 1 opens the ports; Article 2 fixes the payment; and only then does Article 3 say "We grant, on these conditions, by the present ordinance ... the full and entire independence of their Government." Independence arrives third, conditional on the first two. Contemporaries saw it: the New-York American objected that the decree "purports to open, in virtue of the sovereign authority of the King of France, the ports and harbors of the French part of St. Domingo ... without ever referring to the existing government of Hayti", and that it conceded "privileges to what is still called a colony, and over which the ultimate dominion is in no wise renounced". The following year's Convention had to "explain the ambiguity in the first paragraph of the first article of the Ordinance" — the objection was correct.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall is priced out loud by the French royalist press, and the arithmetic is the most useful sentence in the whole record. From the Étoile of 13 August 1825: "It was calculated that the revenue of the colonists was thirty millions.—Deducting the half for the expenses of cultivation, there remain fifteen millions. The one hundred and fifty millions which the King has de[cree]d that the inhabitants of St. Domingo shall pay into the Caisse des Depots, make therefore, ten years of the revenue of the ancient colonists; and landed property sells at no higher price throughout the Antilles." The indemnity was set as ten years' capitalisation of the net income stream the colonists had been taking from enslaved labour. And the thing being paid for was in large part already Haitian: "a very large part of the alienated estates of the Ex-Colonists is now owned by the Hay[ti]en government."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment was the ceremony, and it was thorough. Across two independent American reprints of the reception at Port-au-Prince — the shore reception, the march to the Senate with two rear-admirals and martial music, the examination and admission of the act, Mackau's address, the Senate President's reply, the ratification dinner, a second dinner by the Government, a fête aboard the Eylau, a ball by the French residents, and the toasts to Charles X and the Dauphin — NOT ONE FRANC IS MENTIONED. Mackau called it "the most generous treaty of which the age affords an example", and in the other translation "the most generous compact of which the present era offers a[n example]". President Boyer's own proclamation to the Haitian people of 11 July 1825 announces that "A special ordinance of his Majesty Charles X., dated the 17th of April last, recognizes the full and entire Independence of your Government", promises that "Commerce and agriculture will now be greatly extended", closes "Live forever, Liberty, Liberty" — and contains no sum, no instalment, no creditor and no Caisse.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The claims of the dispossessed colonists of Saint-Domingue, and a French domestic precedent the royalist press named in the same breath: "The Monarch, who has just closed the last wounds of the revolution, by indemnifying the emigrants, could not forget one of the greatest misfortunes produced by it." The Haitian indemnity was presented as the colonial instalment of a programme already run at home.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A recognition instrument that is simultaneously a tariff schedule and a debt instrument, payable into a French state deposit fund — and, within a year, a Convention adding that "Hayti shall remain neutral in all maritime wars", that "no Haytien citizen or vessel shall visit French colonies", and that French warships may enter Haitian ports with the Haitian government's consent. Sovereignty recognised and then specified away, article by article.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The revenue once extracted from enslaved labour is capitalised at ten years' purchase and reimposed as a debt on the people who ended it; the debt's first instalment falls due in eight months; the same instrument halves the duties paid by the creditor nation's shipping, so the trade that must generate the payment is taxed in the creditor's favour; and the estates being paid for are substantially owned by the paying state already.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That France extorted independence from Haiti at gunpoint for 150 million francs, and that the sum was an arbitrary figure plucked to cripple the first Black republic — or, in the opposite telling, that the 1825 ordonnance was a magnanimous recognition freely given, as its own envoy described it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The record read here refuses both, and it refuses them with documents from each side printed on the same page. AGAINST THE MAGNANIMITY STORY: the ordonnance's own Article 3 grants independence "on these conditions" — third, after the tariff and after the 150,000,000 francs — and the New-York American said so within weeks, objecting that the decree never refers to "the existing government of Hayti" and concedes privileges to "what is still called a colony, and over which the ultimate dominion is in no wise renounced". That objection was vindicated by events: the Convention of the following year had to "explain the ambiguity in the first paragraph of the first article of the Ordinance". AGAINST THE ARBITRARY-FIGURE STORY: the sum was not arbitrary and the French royalist press published the method. Thirty millions of annual colonial revenue, less half for the costs of cultivation, leaves fifteen; "The one hundred and fifty millions ... make therefore, ten years of the revenue of the ancient colonists". It was a capitalisation, calculated, and defended in print on the ground that "landed property sells at no higher price throughout the Antilles". A considered price for a stream of income from slavery is worse than an arbitrary one, not better. AND ON THE GUNPOINT: no coercion is documented in what was read. What is documented is a squadron, two rear-admirals, martial music, and a ceremony in which the price was never said aloud — not in Mackau's address, not in the Senate President's reply, not in Boyer's proclamation to his own people, not in the toasts. THE ONE THING THIS DOSSIER STILL CANNOT DO is follow the money. Nothing read establishes what was actually paid, when, or through what borrowing; the 1826 loan, the later reductions and the long service of the debt are all outside it. LIMITS OF SOURCING, STATED PLAINLY: every source here is an American newspaper reprint read as the Library of Congress's OCR transcription, not as a page image, and not as a French archival original — gallica.bnf.fr serves a bot-verification challenge to scripts and to the browser alike and was not circumvented, so the sealed instrument itself has not been seen. The 150,000,000 figure is therefore carried by cross-check rather than by one reading: four pages across three papers print it in francs and a fifth prints the dollar equivalent, with the instalment structure agreeing across them.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The text of the Ordonnance of Charles X of 17 April 1825, reprinted from the official part of the Paris Moniteur of 12 August 1825 in the Phenix Gazette (Alexandria, D.C.) of 17 September 1825, in three articles: the ports of the French part of St Domingo opened to the commerce of all nations with duties equal for all flags except the French, whose duties are halved; the present inhabitants to pay into the Caisse générale des Dépôts et des Consignations, in five equal yearly instalments beginning 31 December 1825, 150,000,000 francs to indemnify the ancient colonists who claim an indemnity; and, "on these conditions", the grant of full and entire independence. Signed by Charles and countersigned by the Ministers of Marine and Colonies and of Justice and the President of the Council. The figure is corroborated in the Constitutional Whig of 20 September 1825, the Phenix Gazette of 27 February 1826, the Richmond Enquirer of 2 March 1826, and in dollars — "Thirty Millions of dollars—one fifth part to be paid on the 31st December next, and the other four parts in annual instalments" — in the Edwardsville Spectator of 3 September 1825, which also reports that fifty millions of dollars had first been asked, that the sum was to pay the colonists' claims "in part", and that "a very large part of the alienated estates of the Ex-Colonists is now owned by the Hay[ti]en government". The Étoile of 13 August 1825, reprinted alongside the ordonnance, derives the sum as ten years of the ancient colonists' net revenue and calls Haiti's acceptance "this act of submission, this recognition of the sovereignty of France". The New-York American, on the same page, objects that the decree does not refer to the existing government of Hayti and cannot be urged as a full and free recognition of independence. The reception at Port-au-Prince is reported in two independent translations — the Concord Register of 20 August 1825 and the Richmond Enquirer of 19 August 1825 — comprising Boyer's proclamation of 11 July 1825, Mackau's description of "the most generous treaty of which the age affords an example", M. Guyot's reply on behalf of the Senate, and the subsequent dinners, fête and toasts; none of these mentions any payment. The Richmond Enquirer of 4 March 1826 summarises the ensuing Convention, whose first article "explains the ambiguity in the first paragraph of the first article of the Ordinance" while retaining a reserve, limits the French commercial advantage to French goods in French ships direct from France, halves differential duties on Haitian produce, provides that no Haitian citizen or vessel shall visit French colonies, admits French warships to Haitian ports with Haitian consent, and requires that Haiti remain neutral in all maritime wars.

citations.title: "Ordinance of the King", Charles X, Paris, 17 April 1825, reprinted from the Paris Moniteur of 12 August 1825 (Official Part) — Phenix Gazette (Alexandria, D.C.), 17 September 1825, page 2
citations.quoteOrFact: HOW THIS WAS READ, STATED FIRST BECAUSE IT MATTERS. The Library of Congress's Chronicling America HTML pages sit behind a bot-verification interstitial that returns HTTP 403 to scripted requests and was not circumvented — it also blocks the browser pane. What was read is the Library's OWN public machine interface for the same page: the resource JSON at this URL with `&fo=json`, and the full-text endpoint it names at tile.loc.gov (`text-services/word-coordinates-service ... &format=alto_xml&full_text=1`), which serve to a request declaring an identity and contact address. SO WHAT WAS READ IS THE LIBRARY'S OCR TRANSCRIPTION OF THE SCANNED PAGE, NOT THE PAGE IMAGE. The page image was not inspected. The OCR is visibly imperfect and some names are mangled; reconstructions are marked in square brackets below and nothing is quoted that depends on a doubtful character. THE TEXT OF THE ORDONNANCE, as the Moniteur's official part printed it: "Baron de M[ac]kau in the navy, sailed from Rochefort on the 4th of May last, on board the Circe frigate, with orders to proceed to St. Domingo, and to carry thither the following ordinance: ORDINANCE OF THE KING. Paris, April 17. Charles, by the Grace of God, [King] of France and Navarre. To all to whom these presents shall come, greeting: Considering articles 14 and 73 of the Charter, desiring to provide for what is called for by the interests of the French merchants, the misfortunes of the ancient colonies of St. Domingo, and the precarious situation of the present inhabitants of that island: We have ordained and ordain as follows: Art. 1. The ports of the French part of St Domingo are open to the commerce of all nations. The duties levied in the ports, either upon vessels or merchandise, whether entering or going out, shall be equal and uniform for all flags except for the French flag, in favor of which these duties shall be reduced one half. 2. The present inhabitants of the French part of St. Domingo shall pay into the Caisse [générale des Dépôts et] des Consignations of France, in five equal instalments, from year to year, the first of which will become due on the 31st of December, 1825, the sum of 150,000,000 of francs, destined to indemnify the ancient colonists who shall claim an indemnity. 3. We grant, on these conditions, by the present ordinance, to the actual inhabitants of the French part of the island of St Domingo, the full and entire independence of their Government." Sealed with the great seal; given at the Tuileries, 17 April 1825, "and in the first of our reign"; signed "By the King, CHARLES", countersigned by the Minister of Marine and Colonies (printed "Count deC1IARROL" — Chabrol), the Keeper of the Seals ("Count dePEYRONNET"), and the President of the Council of Ministers ("M. [de] VILLELE"). THE FIGURE WAS CROSS-CHECKED, because a single OCR of a single number is not enough. Four further Library of Congress pages were pulled by the same route and independently print it: Constitutional Whig (Richmond), 20 September 1825, page 2 (/resource/sn83045110/1825-09-20/ed-1/?sp=2) — "the 31st of December, 1[8]25, the sum of 150,000,000 of" francs; Phenix Gazette, 27 February 1826, page 2 — "that 150,000,000 of francs have been agreed to"; Richmond Enquirer, 2 March 1826, page 2 — "it is understood that 150,000,0[0]0 of francs have"; and the dollar equivalent appears independently in the Edwardsville Spectator of 3 September 1825 as "Thirty Millions of dollars—one fifth part". Two different units in different papers agreeing at roughly five francs to the dollar, and a fifth part matching the five annual instalments. THE SAME PAGE CARRIES THE OBJECTION, MADE IN 1825, which is why this citation is worth more than the ordonnance alone. From the New-York American: "The independence of Hayti, the formal recognition of which, by France, has been thought worth thirty millions of dollars, would seem after all, by the following documents ... not to have been frankly and honestly acknowledged by the French government. The royal decree purports to open, in virtue of the sovereign authority of the King of France, the ports and harbors of the French part of St. Domingo, to the trade of all nations; and makes various provisions relative thereto, without ever referring to the existing government of Hayti." And: "this concession by France, for it is scarcely any thing more, of privileges to what is still called a colony, and over which the ultimate dominion is in no wise renounced, cannot be urged to any foreign nation by way of precedent, as a full and free recognition of independence. It is in cases like these, that forms become substance, and that the withholding, or qualifying a word, or a phrase, become more important than millions of money, or years of warfare." AND THE SAME PAGE CARRIES THE FRENCH ROYALIST ANSWER, which prices the indemnity out loud. From the Étoile of 13 August 1825, reprinted alongside: "It was calculated that the revenue of the colonists was thirty millions.—Deducting the half for the expenses of cultivation, there remain fifteen millions. The one hundred and fifty millions which the King has de[cree]d that the inhabitants of St. Domingo shall pay into the Caisse des Depots, make therefore, ten years of the revenue of the ancient colonists; and landed property sells at no higher price throughout the Antilles." The Étoile then characterises what Haiti had done: "All the efforts of Bonaparte had failed in an enterprise, the advantages of which, even after having succeeded, could not be equivalent to what some words of the King have produced. It is with respect and gratitude that the inhabitants of the French part of St. Domingo have received the orders of their King, and it is not till after this act of submission, this recognition of the sovereignty of France that the" [sentence continues beyond the column read]. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED HERE: no French archival original was read — gallica.bnf.fr serves a bot-verification challenge to scripts and to the browser pane alike and was not circumvented — so this is a newspaper reprint of an official gazette, two removes from the sealed instrument. Nothing here establishes what was actually paid, when, or by what borrowing.

citations.title: "AFFAIRS OF HAYTI" — Proclamation of President Jean-Pierre Boyer, National Palace, Port-au-Prince, 11 July 1825, with the addresses of Baron de Mackau; Concord Register (Concord, N.H.), 20 August 1825, page 3
citations.quoteOrFact: Read as the Library of Congress's OCR transcription, via its own resource JSON and tile.loc.gov full-text endpoint (the HTML page is bot-walled to automated requests and was not circumvented); the page image was not inspected. The OCR mangles names and accents — the signature prints as "Joun PierrE BovEßr" for Jean-Pierre Boyer — and nothing is quoted that turns on a doubtful character. THE WHOLE POINT OF THIS CITATION IS WHAT THE PROCLAMATION DOES NOT SAY. Boyer's address to the Haitian people, "Given at the National Palace, Port-au-Prince, 11th July, 1825, and twenty-second year of Independence", announces the ordonnance and never mentions the money: "A long oppression had borne down Hayti: Your courage and your heroic efforts, raised her, twenty years since, from degradation to the rank of independent nations. But your glory demands other trium[ph]. The French Flag, coming this day to salute the land of liberty, consec[rat]es the legitimacy of your emancipation. It was reserved to the monarch of France, not less religious than great, to signalize his advance[ment] to the crown by an act of justice, which at once adds brilliancy to the throne from which it emanates, and to the nation which is its object. Haytiens! A special ordinance of his Majesty Charles X., dated the 17th of April last, recognizes the full and entire Independence of your Government. This authentic act, by adding the formality of law to the political existence which you have already acquired, will give you that rank in the world, in which you have been placed, and to which divine Providence calls you." It promises that "Commerce and agriculture will now be greatly extended" and closes "Live forever, Liberty, Liberty. Live forever, Independence". There is no sum, no instalment, no creditor and no Caisse anywhere in it. THE ENVOY'S OWN DESCRIPTION OF THE TERMS, to the Haitian Senate: "The King has ordered me to come and offer in his name, the most generous treaty of which the age affords an example. You here find proof, gentlemen, that under these weighty circumstances the royal mind is not less bent towards the preca[ri]ous situation of Hay[ti], than the interests of his own subjects." He then "laid the decree on the table of the President of the Senate". Addressing Boyer directly, Mackau reported his instructions: "The King has said to me, [g]o to this celebrated Man, offer [h]im peace, and [h]is country happiness and prosperity. I have obeyed,—I have met the Man who was designated by my master, and Hayti has taken her rank amongst the independent nations." WHAT THE PAPER REPORTS HAPPENED NEXT, which is the ceremony without the price: "On Monday, the day of the ratification of the Ordinance, a dinner was given to Baron Mackau, at the house of the Secretary of State; and on Wednesday another by the Government. In addition to this, a fete was given by Admiral Ju[ri]en on board the Eylau, where were a great number of public officers and a few ladies. The French who were at Port-au-Prince, previously to the recognition, gave a dinner and ball in honor of the event." Among the toasts recorded: "By the Secretary General.—His Majesty Charles X. King of France and Navarre, his son the Dauphin, and the Royal Family. May this family reign forever in France for the happiness of the nation and the honor of humanity!" NOT A FRANC IS MENTIONED IN ANY OF IT. The dateline on the column is "New-York, August 12", so this is a reprint of documents received in New York, not a Haitian imprint; no Haitian government publication was read.

citations.title: Reception of the royal ordonnance by the Senate of Haiti: addresses of Baron de Mackau and of M. Guyot, President of the Senate — Richmond Enquirer (Richmond, Va.), 19 August 1825, page 2
citations.quoteOrFact: Read as the Library of Congress's OCR transcription via its own JSON and full-text endpoints; the page image was not inspected and the OCR is degraded in places. This is a SECOND, INDEPENDENT translation of the same ceremony reported in the Concord Register, and it confirms the same absence. THE SCENE: "Early in the morning, agreeably to notice, the civil and military authorities met on the sea shore, where they received the Baron de M[a]ckau, bearer of the royal Ord[o]nance by which his M[ost] C[hristian] M[ajesty] Charles X. acknowledges fully and absolutely the independence of the Republic of Hayti. The Baron de Mackau, with Rear Admirals Ju[ri]en and Grivel on each side, preceded by the officers of the French squadron, and at the sound of martial music, proceeded to the Senate, where the examination and admission of the act of recognition took place." MACKAU'S ADDRESS, here rendered "compact" rather than "treaty": "The King has commanded me to come towards you, and to offer you in his name the most generous compact of which the present era offers a[n example] ... You [will find] in it, Gentlemen, the proof that his Majesty has not less been bent upon the precarious state of the Haytians, than upon the interests of his own subjects." He adds: "God will bless, gentlemen, this sincere and [di]rect reconciliation, and will permit that it shall serve as an example to other states still torn by evils shocking to humanity." THE REPLY OF THE PRESIDENT OF THE SENATE, M. Guyot: "We receive with veneration, the ordonnance of his Most Christian Majesty, by which the recognition of the independence of Hayti is formally declared, and which you have been intrusted to present to us. It belonged to one of the descendants of the noble and ancient race of the Bourbons to put the seal to the great work of our regeneration, after so many fatal and cruel calamities. Charles X. justly styled Most Christian King, has at length acknowledged the right acquired by the Haytian people, and calls this young nation to rank among the ancient nations." And: "Gl[o]ry be to the August Monarch, who disdaining the laurels which would be stained with blood, has preferred to gird his majesty's brow with the olive of peace." Closing: "The name of his Sovereign, that of the Dauphin of France, and his own, shall be inscribed in indelible traits in the records of Hayti." IN THE WHOLE OF THE CEREMONY AS REPORTED — the shore, the march, the Senate, both speeches and the reply — THERE IS NO MENTION OF 150,000,000 FRANCS, of instalments, or of any payment at all. That is the finding this citation carries, and it is a finding about silence, which is why it is corroborated here by a second paper rather than rested on one.

citations.title: "FRANCE AND HAYTI" — additional particulars of the indemnity arrangements; Edwardsville Spectator (Edwardsville, Ill.), 3 September 1825, page 2
citations.quoteOrFact: Read as the Library of Congress's OCR transcription via its own JSON and full-text endpoints; the page image was not inspected. This is the terms stated in dollars, in a paper a thousand miles from the capital, and it corroborates the francs figure in the Phenix Gazette independently. ON THE FORM OF THE ACT: "The Ordinance of France, acknowledging the Independence of Hay[ti], was communicated immediately on the ratification of the Treaty, with parade and formality, to the Hay[ti]en Senate; by whom it was enregistered and proclaimed, agreeably to the Constitution of the Republic." ON THE AMOUNT AND THE SCHEDULE: "It appears to be confirmed that the indemnification to France, agreed upon, is Thirty Millions of dollars—one fifth part to be paid on the 31st December next, and the other four parts in annual instalments." ON WHAT WAS FIRST DEMANDED: "This sum is a large one, but it is believed was not the maximum demanded by France at the commencement of the negotiation and that f[if]ty millions were asked". ON WHAT THE MONEY WAS FOR: "It is to be appropriated to the payment, in part, of the large amount of claims of the Ex-Colonists of St. D[o]mingo, for their losses." IN PART — the paper's own qualifier; the 150,000,000 francs did not purport to discharge the claims in full. ON WHAT HAITI ALREADY OWNED, which is the detail that makes the transaction legible: "Large as the indemnity to be given by Hayti is, we are assured that the finances of the Republic are equal to its prompt payment, and a very large part of the alienated estates of the Ex-Colonists is now owned by the Hay[ti]en government." Haiti was to pay for property its own state already held. THE PAPER ALSO REPEATS A RUMOUR, recorded here as a rumour and nothing more: "it has been asserted, that when C[h]ristoph[e] died he left ten millions of dollars, in spe[c]ie, in his vaults at Sans Souci". THE CONFIDENCE ABOUT HAITI'S CAPACITY TO PAY IS THE PAPER'S, NOT A FINDING: "we are assured that the finances of the Republic are equal to its prompt payment" is reported belief in September 1825, three months before the first instalment fell due. Nothing in this page establishes whether any instalment was paid, or how.

citations.title: "Of the Convention we learn the following authentic particulars" — the Franco-Haitian Convention concluded at Paris, reported from the National Gazette; Richmond Enquirer (Richmond, Va.), 4 March 1826, page 4
citations.quoteOrFact: Read as the Library of Congress's OCR transcription via its own JSON and full-text endpoints; the page image was not inspected. WHY THIS CITATION EXISTS: it records that the ordonnance's grant of independence was ambiguous enough to require a further instrument to fix — which is precisely what the New-York American had objected in September 1825, and it is the vindication of that objection in the following year's news. THE FIRST ARTICLE, in the paper's summary: "The first article of this document explains the ambiguity in the first paragraph of the first article of the Ordinance, and acknowledges the entire independence of the country, with the reserve made in the second paragraph of the same article." An ambiguity, explained; and a reserve, retained. THE COMMERCIAL ARTICLES: "The second article regulates the extent of advantages conferred on French commerce, and limits them to French manufactures and produce, the property of Frenchmen, imp[ort]ed in French bottoms direct from France, and to the returns of the same ... The third article favors Haytien produce, imported in French and Haytien bottoms [to] one half the differential duties paid on West India produce imported from other than French colonies. The fourth article provides for the negotiation of a trea[t]y placing the navigation of each country on an equal footing." THE ARTICLES ABOUT WHERE HAITIANS AND THE FRENCH NAVY MAY GO: "The fifth assu[r]es amicable treatment of the Haytien flag on the ocean by all French men of war, and provides that no Haytien citizen or vessel shall visit French colonies. The sixth treats of the admission of French men of war in Haytien ports; not, however, without the consen[t] of the Haytien government." AND THE NEUTRALITY CLAUSE: "The twentieth specifies that Hayti shall remain neutral in all maritime wars; and in case of being herself involved the French monarch promises his m[e]diation." A state whose independence had just been granted was to stay neutral in all maritime wars, and could not send its citizens or ships to French colonies. ON THE STATE OF THE PROCESS: the Convention had been concluded by the Haitian commissioners sent to France "but [was] not yet officially communicated to the Haytien councils", its return reportedly delayed by the death of one of the commissioners. SO THE CONVENTION'S OWN TEXT WAS NOT READ: these are a newspaper's "authentic particulars" of an instrument not yet published in Haiti, article by article, in summary. Nothing here restates the 150,000,000 francs or alters it, and nothing here establishes what was ratified.
